title: HE ONLY PICKED UP STICKS—THEN MOSES ORDERED HIS DEATH
paragraphs: HE ONLY PICKED UP STICKS—THEN MOSES ORDERED HIS DEATH
The terrifying story in Numbers 15:32–36 was never really about a handful of wood. And if you read it too quickly, you may miss the warning… and the grace… hiding in plain sight.
He was only gathering sticks.
That is what makes the story so disturbing.
Not murdering someone.
Not stealing gold.
Not bowing before an idol in the middle of the camp.
Sticks.
A man bent down on the Sabbath and gathered pieces of wood from the wilderness floor.
Someone saw him.
Then someone else.
Before long, they brought him before Moses, Aaron, and the congregation.
And the ending is difficult to read.
The man died.
If you have ever reached Numbers 15:32–36 and quietly wondered, Why was the punishment so severe? you are not irreverent for noticing how shocking the passage is.
You are supposed to feel its weight.
But before we accuse God of punishing a man for something as trivial as picking up firewood, we need to slow down and read what Scripture actually says.
Because the sticks were visible.
The deeper issue was rebellion.
And that changes everything.
Numbers 15:32 begins:
וַיִּהְיוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּמִּדְבָּר וַיִּמְצְאוּ אִישׁ מְקֹשֵׁשׁ עֵצִים בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת
Vayihyu v’nei-Yisra’el bamidbar, vayimtze’u ish meqoshesh etzim b’yom haShabbat.
In context: “While the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day.”
The Hebrew word מְקֹשֵׁשׁ — meqoshesh describes the man as gathering or collecting.
Nothing in that word, by itself, makes the act look dramatic.
And that is precisely why context matters.
This incident does not appear in isolation.
Immediately before it, God had distinguished between unintentional sin and something very different.
Numbers 15:30 describes the person who sins בְּיָד רָמָה — b’yad ramah.
Literally, the expression carries the picture of acting “with a high hand.”
Defiantly.
Presumptuously.
Openly setting oneself against the command of God.
Then comes the chilling explanation in verse 31:
כִּי דְבַר־יְהוָה בָּזָה וְאֶת־מִצְוָתוֹ הֵפַר
Ki devar-YHWH bazah, v’et-mitzvato hefar.
“For he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken His commandment.”
Then, immediately afterward, Scripture tells us about the man gathering wood on the Sabbath.
That placement matters.
The narrative invites us to read the incident against the distinction that has just been made between inadvertent wrongdoing and deliberate defiance.
This was not Israel accidentally discovering that God disliked firewood.
The Sabbath command had already been given.
Israel had already been told:
זָכוֹר אֶת־יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ
Zakhor et-yom haShabbat leqaddesho.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”
Exodus 20:8.
And Exodus 31:14–15 had already attached an extraordinarily serious covenant penalty to profaning the Sabbath.
So when Numbers says the man was found gathering wood on that day, the issue was not the market value of the sticks.
The issue was what his action represented within Israel’s covenant relationship with God.
Sometimes rebellion does not look dramatic.
Sometimes rebellion looks ordinary.
That may be the uncomfortable part of this story.
We tend to measure sin by appearance.
God sees the heart from which it comes.
We say:
“It was only one lie.”
“It was only one message.”
“It was only one night.”
“It was only bitterness.”
“It was only pornography.”
“It was only gossip.”
“It was only money.”
“It was only flirting.”
“It was only something nobody knows about.”
“It was only…”
Sticks.
And suddenly this ancient man in the wilderness does not feel quite so distant.
Because human beings have become extraordinarily skilled at shrinking what God has said so that disobedience feels manageable.
We rename greed “ambition.”
We rename lust “chemistry.”
We rename vengeance “closure.”
We rename pride “knowing my worth.”
We rename compromise “being realistic.”
We rename spiritual apathy “being busy.”
And sometimes we rename deliberate disobedience “a mistake” because mistake hurts less than rebellion.
But Numbers 15 will not allow us to hide forever behind softer vocabulary.
There is another detail people often miss.
Verse 34 says:
וַיַּנִּיחוּ אֹתוֹ בַּמִּשְׁמָר כִּי לֹא פֹרַשׁ מַה־יֵּעָשֶׂה לוֹ
They placed him in custody because it had not yet been made clear what should be done to him.
Think about that.
They did not simply become enraged and execute him on impulse.
They detained him.
They waited.
Then the LORD gave Moses the judgment recorded in the text.
Numbers 15:35–36 says that the man was to be put to death outside the camp, and the congregation carried out the sentence as the LORD had commanded Moses.
It is severe.
We should not sanitize it.
Neither should we detach it from its covenant setting and pretend the passage teaches Christians to execute Sabbath violators today.
It does not.
Ancient Israel existed under the Mosaic covenant as a covenant nation with civil, ceremonial, and moral dimensions intertwined in ways that do not simply transfer wholesale to the church.
Jesus’ apostles did not establish Christian congregations by reproducing Israel’s civil penalties.
But neither should we swing to the opposite extreme and conclude that the story has nothing to say to us.
Because the holiness of God has not disappeared.
And sin has not become harmless.
The Bible does something astonishing with that truth.
It takes us from a man condemned outside the camp…
to another Man who suffered outside the gate.
Hebrews 13:12 says:
“Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.”
Do not rush past that.
The guilty man of Numbers 15 was taken outside the camp and received judgment.
Then, centuries later, Jesus Christ—the sinless Son of God—went outside the gate bearing shame He did not deserve.
This does not mean Numbers 15 is a direct prophecy predicting the crucifixion.
We should not force Scripture to say something it does not say.
But when the whole biblical story is allowed to speak, the contrast is breathtaking.
We are the rebels.
Christ is the righteous One.
We broke God's commands.
Christ obeyed perfectly.
We deserved judgment.
Christ willingly bore judgment for sinners.
The gospel does not announce that sin was never serious.
The cross announces that sin was so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
That is why grace is not God shrugging His shoulders and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace says it mattered more than we could imagine…
and Jesus paid what we could never pay.
Isaiah had written of the suffering servant:
וַיהוָה הִפְגִּיעַ בּוֹ אֵת עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ
VaYHWH hifgia bo et avon kullanu.
“The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Isaiah 53:6.
Then the New Testament brings the scandal of grace into terrifying clarity.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:21:
τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν
Ton mē gnonta hamartian hyper hēmōn hamartian epoiēsen.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin…”
So that in Christ we might become the righteousness of God.
That is Christianity.
Not good people proving that they deserve heaven.
Not religious people pretending they never gathered their own metaphorical sticks.
Not sinners hiding behind church attendance while secret rebellion consumes them.
Christianity begins with the devastating confession:
I have sinned.
And then comes the sentence Satan does not want the repentant sinner to believe:
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Maybe your “sticks” have a name.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you can sing on Sunday while carrying it.
Maybe you preach.
Maybe you lead.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
God already sees behind the profile.
Behind the ministry.
Behind the smile.
Behind the excuses.
And yet the gospel invitation remains.
Repent.
Come home.
Not because your sin is small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
The Greek word so often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō: to repent, to change one's mind, to turn in response to the truth.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Peter wept bitterly.
But repentance is more than emotion.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And the good news is that you do not clean yourself up enough to become worthy of Jesus.
You come because you are not worthy.
You come because He is merciful.
You come because the crucified and risen Christ is the only Savior sinners have.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice the astonishing word.
Just.
How can a holy God forgive guilty people and remain just?
The answer stands on a hill outside Jerusalem.
The cross.
Jesus did not manipulate justice.
He satisfied it.
Romans 3:26 describes God as both “just” and the “justifier” of the one who has faith in Jesus.
The Judge Himself provided the rescue.
This is why the man gathering sticks should disturb us.
And this is why Jesus should overwhelm us.
We often want a God holy enough to punish everyone who has wounded us but lenient enough to overlook everything hidden inside us.
The Bible gives us something infinitely more frightening and infinitely more beautiful.
A God who is truly holy.
A humanity that is truly guilty.
A judgment that is truly deserved.
And a Savior who truly died and truly rose.
At Calvary, God did not pretend rebellion was harmless.
Christ bore sin's curse so that rebels who repent and believe could be reconciled to God.
That is scandalous grace.
Maybe you have spent years believing your history disqualified you.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Sexual sin.
Anger.
Abortion.
Adultery.
Pride.
A secret habit.
Years wasted running from God.
Words you cannot take back.
People you cannot unhurt.
Things you desperately wish you could erase.
Listen carefully.
The gospel does not give you a time machine.
It gives you a Redeemer.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending your sin never happened.
He rewrites what happens to the sinner who comes to Him.
Condemned becomes forgiven.
Far away becomes brought near.
Slave becomes free.
Enemy becomes reconciled.
Dead becomes alive.
Ashamed becomes clothed in Christ.
Not because the sinner became impressive.
Because Jesus is enough.
Maybe that is why you needed to find this article today.
Not to stare at a dead man holding sticks.
But to finally look at the living Christ with empty hands.
Stop negotiating.
Stop hiding.
Stop telling God, “It was only…”
He knows.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
And when you fall, do not turn grace into permission to remain in sin.
Run back to Jesus.
Grace is not a comfortable hiding place for rebellion.
Titus 2:11–12 says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Jesus did not die merely to make sinners feel less guilty while leaving them chained to what was destroying them.
He came to save.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Come back and remember.
God is holy.
Sin matters.
Jesus saves.
And grace is costly beyond imagination.
Not as a performance of righteousness and never as a way of earning God's favor.
Send it privately to the friend who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that repentance is still possible and Christ still receives sinners.
Supporting Gospel work should come from willing generosity, not spiritual pressure.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is still gathering sticks.
Somebody is still saying, “It is only this once.”
Somebody is still hiding.
Somebody believes the secret is too ugly to confess.
Somebody thinks judgment is the end of their story.
And somebody needs to hear that the same Bible that refuses to trivialize sin also announces a Savior whose grace reaches repentant sinners in places shame told them God would never enter.
The story in Numbers ends outside the camp with a sinner under judgment.
But the Bible does not end there.
Outside another city…
outside another gate…
stood a cross.
And on that cross hung the One who had never rebelled.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
And still calling sinners home.
So put down the sticks.
Stop hiding your hands.
Stop defending what is killing you.
Bring your sin into the light.
Come to Christ.
Because the most unforgettable thing about your story does not have to be the scandal of what you did.
It can be the grace of the One who saved you.
The sticks may reveal the rebellion—but the scars in His hands reveal how far grace was willing to go to bring the rebel home.
